newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai stores cash in on Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai stores cash in on Christmas.

text.p: Shanghai department stores are cashing in on Christmas to exploit young, fashion-conscious consumers' appetite for Western ideas and products, retail officials said on Friday.
Christmas promotions are more pervasive and lavish than ever before with stores working hard to convince customers to buy trees, decorations, cards and gifts.
In short, they want an earlier start to China's traditional spending boom that precedes the Chinese New Year in late January or early February.

Shanghai is China's biggest single retail market, with sales in the first 11 months this year of 105.561 billion yuan ($12.7 billion), up 19.8 percent from the same 1995 period, or 14 percent if adjusted for inflation, official figures show.
"The idea of Christmas as a time for gifts, cards and celebrations is growing year by year among young people," said Tong Shenjie, head of the information department of Kai Kai Plaza.
Kai Kai, a seven-storey department store, features Christmas trees, cards and decorations at its entrance.
"December and January are the peak period for sales, with daily volume at one million yuan, up from a daily 500,000 to 600,000 yuan in November," Tong said.

A spokesman for a $200 million joint venture department store majority owned by Yaohan International Holding said that December was a bumper period, with daily sales rising at least 50 percent over the average level, with Christmas the main factor.
The store has arranged a Christmas/New Year promotion, giving away a 50-yuan gift certificate for each 500 yuan worth of goods bought, he said.
"The period just before the Lunar New Year remains the period of biggest spending for Chinese," said Shi Jianxing, a manager at the Taiwan-invested Mosta department store.

"But the golden season has been extended into December with spending on Christmas cards, decorations and gifts," he said. "The Christmas factor will boost sales. There is no religious feeling. It is just commercial."
Store staff said the main Christmas consumers were students and people in their 20s, who spent up to several hundred yuan each.

"This all started three years ago," said a saleswoman at Mosta's Christmas gift counter. "Christmas spending has become a fashion. Schools and firms, especially those with foreign investment, put on Christmas parties."

"I plan to spend about 500 yuan this year on cards and presents for my friends," said Wang Hongjun, a salesman in his 20s. "We young people in Shanghai like to copy Western habits. But older people spend nothing on Christmas. They will save up their gifts for Chinese New Year."

But Christmas cheer was not so warm at the state-run Number One Department Store in northwest Shanghai. There is a life-size Santa Claus wrapped in plastic at the main door, but almost no other signs of festive spirit.
"Christmas is not a national holiday and there is no promotion of it in the media," said Luo Huakun, sales department manager. "That means that the atmosphere is not so lively.
"It is during Chinese New Year that we have to give presents to people even if we do not want to," he added.
